idiom_name: per-type copy function (struct assignment + deep-copy routine), optionally behind a type-descriptor vtable
implementation_notes: C has no classes, no copy constructors and no polymorphic clone, so the pattern is hand-written. A plain structure assignment (*dst = *src) copies every member but aliases every pointer, so a prototype copy must be paired with a per-type deep-copy function that reallocates owned buffers and recurses into nested structures. When callers need to clone through a common handle - the polymorphic case the pattern is really about - put a clone function pointer in a per-type ops descriptor (struct shape_ops { struct shape *(*clone)(const struct shape *); ... }) and treat that descriptor as the Prototype interface; a registry then maps a name to a descriptor plus the configured exemplar. Every clone needs a matching destroy/ownership rule, otherwise responsibility for the copied buffers is undefined. Where only one concrete type exists, skip the vtable and write the copy function directly.
pitfalls: *dst = *src (and memcpy) is a shallow copy: char* buffers, arrays and nested structs are aliased, and freeing both copies double-frees.
Without a paired destroy function and a documented owner per pointed-to field, a clone either leaks memory or frees memory it does not own.
Cloning a prototype that holds a mutex, file descriptor or socket duplicates the handle value, not the resource; such state must be shared or re-initialised explicitly.
A descriptor pointer copied into the clone must point at a static/shared ops table - cloning the descriptor itself breaks function pointer identity.
